titleStmt.title: Interview with Phillip C. Vincello, April 27, 2003
titleStmt.author: Tom Swope

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Phillip C. Vincello was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Phillip C. Vincello. Phil served in the U.S. Army Air Corps with the 385th Bomb Group 551st Squadron. He served in the European Theater. It was a vultured gunner on a B-17, and his highest rank was tech sergeant. I'm Tom Swope. And this recording was made at Mr. Vincello's home in Painesville, Ohio on April 27th, 2002. Phil was 78 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Let's see, Pearl Harbor. Do you remember hearing the news of the attack on Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Answer: I remember the day very well. I was at home living with my folks in Waltham, Mass., and we huddled around the radio and heard that report. Yeah, I remember it very well. Very clearly.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How old were you then -- about then?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Well, let's see, that was in 194- --

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: -- '1. I was born in '23, so that made me 18.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did you think when you heard that news?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: We were shocked. Couldn't believe it. It was unbelievable that anything like that had happened. And we didn't foresee what it meant for us personally. We just thought of the horror of what they had done.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, did you feel the patriotic need to run out there and sign up the next day?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Not at that moment. It wasn't that kind of urgency at that moment, but it certainly came shortly thereafter.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So were you drafted then?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: No. I actually volunteered. I was in college at the time. I was just starting college, I'm sorry. At that point I was just getting ready to start college. And so I volunteered for a reserve group and that's what I did.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When was that?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: In that same year.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: In '42, probably?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Probably '42, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where did you go to college?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: I had did my undergraduate work at Boston College. And I was able to complete three years from my undergraduate work before I was activated. I had joined the Air Force Reserve in the meantime. There were several reserves that came and talked to us, Naval and Army and others. And the Air Force sounded most interesting. And so I had joined the reserve -- the Air Force reserved. At the time I joined the reserve, the idea was that I would be able to graduate and then be activated into the service, but it didn't work that way. At the end of my junior year at college, I was activated and away I went. But on the other hand, that's how -- when I was discharged eventually, with the GI Bill, I was able to go back and finish my last year at Boston College and then I went on to graduate school and took -- and got a law degree at the Harvard Law School.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when were you activated, then?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: The specific date?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Roughly, you know. Let's see, you started school maybe in -- let's try to figure this out -- in '41 maybe?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Yeah. Well, I graduated high school in '40.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: '40. Okay.

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: So in the fall of '40 I must have.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: '40, '41. So it was probably somewhere in '43 you were activated?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Yeah, probably '43.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Spring of '43, around there?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where did you train?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: I did my basic training at a camp -- at a Fort -- Camp -- at a camp in Massachusetts. And then you had to select the specialty, you know, within the Air Force, what you wanted to do. And I wanted to get into armament and that kind of thing, so I ended up in Denver, Colorado, with my -- for that kind of training.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What base was that in Denver? At Lowry?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Had to be Lowry, yes. Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So then you were at gunnery school there?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Well, this was not -- it wasn't the air training. This was the learning the armament. You know, I became what was called an armorer. And my specialty was that I could assemble and disassemble a machine gun blindfolded. That was the final test. If you could do it blindfolded, you could do it. That's what I -- that's where I did that. My air training was in Laredo, Texas, at an air base in Laredo. And that's where I actually got into airplanes and -- and learned the basics of tracking and -- and we -- we -- we practiced with machine guns with cameras on them, of course, obviously. It would have been bad to shoot one of those guys down. Anyhow, we practiced with cameras, and then we would analyze those films after we -- after we got back. So that's where I did my basic air training. Then when I was finally assigned to a crew, we did our crew training in Sioux City, Iowa. And that's where I met my -- my lady who later became my wife.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: She was a Sioux City native?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: She was -- well, she was from South Dakota, but she was working in Sioux City.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when you met the crew, a nice bunch of guys?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Yeah. We got along famously from beginning right on through. We were -- we were very -- very good. Lots of camaraderie. Good people.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How long did you train with that group before you went overseas?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: That was three to six months, I think, and -- yeah, it had to be -- maybe closer to six months that we did that actual training -- flying. And, you know, we did -- we would fly as a crew, and we had sites where we would drop dead bombs, obviously, but -- and then we were graded on those things.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any memorable experiences during training?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: What could top meeting my future wife?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay. The second most memorable thing?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Nothing -- nothing spectacular or different or exciting. It was just -- it was a routine.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: We're talking B-17s, right?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Crew of 10?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And what was your specific job on that?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: And I was the ball turret gunner. And that's where I was graded. I was graded on my activity in that ball turret. Now, also as the armament specialist, I assisted the bombardier if he needed help in arming of armor or hanging bombs or whatever in the bomb bay.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now ball turret, once you were in there, was sealed off, they had a hatch on it?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: It had a hatch, yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It was pretty cramped in there?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Well, I was a lot smaller then than I am today. As a matter of fact, that was one of my goals, is to get out of there and fix it so they could never put me back in.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you eat your way out?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Yeah. You were in there and you were by yourself. You were closed in. There was a hatch door. And the way you entered it from the inside, you would crank the ball so the guns were pointing straight down, open the hatch door, you climbed in, closed the door. And then with the controls, you'd turn the ball and change your position so that your guns are parallel with the bottom of the -- of the airplane.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was it like for the first time you got in there and got in position and flew like that?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: It's called "Hail Mary, full of grace." It was -- it was -- obviously for a city kid from Massachusetts and sitting in that ball turret hanging underneath there and nothing between you and the -- and space except what you were in, it was quite an exciting experience.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did your plane have a name?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: That one -- the one in training did not. The one that we flew in -- the ones that we flew in when we got overseas, they were all named, yeah. But not the ones that we flew in in training.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you go overseas?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: We arrived in the spring of -- or -- February or March. I think it was February or March of '44 is when we flew over. We flew our own airplane over. And that was in -- I think it was March of '44 that we landed in England and we were assigned to a particular base.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you based?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: It -- I wish I could think of the name of that town now.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Near London or...

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: It's southeast of London, yeah, but close enough to London so that on our free time we could take a bus up.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was it like in London -- in England?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Well, of course, it was -- you know, they were being bombed. One of our most -- one of our memorable experiences of being downtown London and -- with my buddies -- no girls, just us guys -- and I'd look up the street and -- we were getting ready to cross the street -- and I looked up the street and standing there with this gorgeous blonde was Jimmy Stewart, who was a pilot. And he was all -- he was all dressed up in his uniform and so were we. And I said -- I nudged the guy, I said, "Look, that's Jimmy out there." And we all turned and crowded and looked up that way. He had planned to come our way. He saw us gawking at him. By the time we looked back, he was galloping across the street with this lady. I could tell you one thing about Jimmy Stewart that I know for sure, he flew many missions, wing to wing, with our -- with our group. And he -- I know he was in some very rough rides because we were in the same place. So they didn't select any special missions for Jimmy. He -- he was right out there in the middle of it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you didn't get a chance to actually talk to Jimmy at any time?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Not at that point. Much later on at a -- at one of those gatherings, I did -- we did get to speak to him. And we kidded him about the fact that we were the guys that saw him running across the street.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any other memorable experiences in England?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: In active -- in the -- in the -- downtown, you know, just visiting the downtown.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's it.

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Can I close this for a minute?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, sure. What was the attitude of the English people toward the Americans over there?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: They were very -- they were very warm to us. They were very friendly and very supportive and very appreciative of the fact that we were there. Yeah, their attitude was great. And we never had any -- I never -- members of our crew, none of us, we never had any problem with them. They were -- they were great. And they were -- they were remarkable people. I -- I was in London on occasions when the bombs would come over. And I'd be running for the subways, but they were much calmer than I was. They would stand and listen to where it was -- you know, they could tell by this time about where it was going to come down and -- but I wasn't waiting. I ran into -- I would run down into the subways. And so many of them would just keep going about their business. They were remarkable people.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So necessarily what we've heard so many times about the Americans being over there, overpaid, oversexed, whatever they used to say?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: No, no. We had very fine reception from them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And as far as the British people in the Army, Air Force, Navy, they were pretty nice, too?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Well, I never really had much commingling with them. You know, we -- we were in our own groups in our own areas, and we didn't commingle with them. So I never had any -- really real contact with them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So how soon after you got there did you fly your first mission?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Well, if I look at my list I can tell you.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's right. Where is that?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: It's in there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: There you go.

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: On April 26th, 1944.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So we've just passed the anniversary of that 58 years ago yesterday.

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Can you imagine?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Yeah. That was our first.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So how long do you think you were there before you flew that mission?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: About a month.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: About a month?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Yeah. Because we did some training there as well, you know. We did some training over England, into -- getting into formations and how -- what to do when we were in formation because we didn't want to be shooting at each other, obviously. And those were tight formations that we flew. So it would be an easy accident to occur, but thank God not for us it didn't happen.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: About how close were you to each other?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Almost wing to wing. And on some of those -- that's -- that's where I -- when I learned to admire our American fighter pilots. We'd be -- the Germans -- the German fighters to attack us would normally group up above us, up -- up above us. And then they would turn down and they'd come down in a string. And literally, time after time, they would come -- they would come right through the shallow holes -- the small holes in our formation, come right on down through. Of course they're shooting all the way. And the -- the thing that we admired and never forgot is that the American fighter pilots -- now our guns are shooting. There's no way to separate what you're shooting at. You're shooting. And the American pilots would be right on their tail coming right down through. Those fighter pilots were fantastic. When I came back to the States after I completed my tour, we came back by ship. And we had some fighter pilots on the same ship. And we spent hours talking to them about their -- their activity. They were a remarkable group. They were fearless.

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Oh, yeah. You know, we flew our own plane over to England. And we had some trouble and we landed at Goose Bay Labrador (ph). And the -- it was -- there was still snow in Goose Bay. And they had these big snow cutters along the side of the runways. And as we were coming down the runway after we had landed, one of our wings caught one of those and it stripped the skin right off the wing. And so the -- the commander of that base came out and caught up with us when we stopped. He was very disturbed that we had done this kind of thing because now we had a B-17 with the skin scraped off and they had no means of repairing it. So they had to fly in another B-17 for us. And that's the one that we took to Europe, is the one they brought in. But the commander of that base was very disturbed.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any particular memories of that first mission you flew?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: No, not -- not the first one. You know, there are several others that you begin -- you remember some of the incidents and stuff.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Go ahead and share memories of other missions you had.

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Well, one of my deepest memories is we were up -- up on the North Sea bombing sub -- subpins, you know. And we really -- we really got hit hard, the flak and the fighters. We were really in bad shape. And at one point we thought we might have to parachute out of there right into the -- into the -- into the sea. And I was not very brave about that. I looked out that door -- you know, we had pulled the door off. I looked out that door and I thought, "Man, that's not where I want to go." But the pilot was trying to determine which would be best for us, whether to go to a neutral country or see if we could get back to England. Anyhow, the decision was made that it would be better for us to go back to England. So we -- we had one engine that was running, one that had a -- had the propeller had run away and it came right out of the cell and went away, and then we had another engine that was -- where the -- where the propeller was just flopping. Anyhow, make a long story short, we -- the pilot felt that the other engines - we had one engine left. It took us back across the channel and on the coast of England is where there was fighter strips. Now, none of our hydraulic systems were working, so we -- he had to land on the belly of the plane. And he did a beautiful job. As a matter of fact, we had a position -- a crash position that we took. My position was to sit in the radio room with my back to the front, you know, and so forth. And we hit the runway and skidded along the runway and it made quite a sound and -- but -- but we landed safely. And then the pilot hollered back from the cockpit, "Get out of here as fast as you can." What had happened is that one propeller that was windmilling, in hitting the runway at whatever -- something caused it to -- that engine caught fire, so the engine -- the airplane had caught fire as we were skidding on the runway. So he said, "Get out of here as fast as you can." So we piled out of there. I'd have to tell you one of my favorite humorous jokes about all that is. So we stood along the side and the ground crews went in and put out the fire and, you know, did all that stuff. And one of the -- one of the members of the ground crew came up, and he ended up standing right beside me. Now, you remember I was a ball turret gunner. He said, "Boy," he said, "I feel so bad for that ball turret gunner." I said, Why? What happened to him?" He said, "Well, you know, underneath there, it was all red. Must have been just lots of blood." The thing he didn't realize is that the hydraulic fluid that worked the ball was red, but I wasn't going to tell him anything different. He said, "Oh, that ball turn gunner, my goodness. I feel so bad for him." I said, "Well, I appreciate your telling me. I'd be sure and let him know." What I was really thinking was, "I'm leaving you with a story you can tell when you get back to the States." But in my mind I'm saying, "That ball turn gunner you're concerned about is here telling you the story." I have -- I have laughs about that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any other memorable missions?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Most of them I -- yeah, I think I told you about the three -- three days in a row to Munich.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Go ahead and tell that on tape so we'll get that.

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Munich was a long air trip for us. It was down in the southeastern part of Germany. And, anyhow, we went down the first day and we did our bombing. There wasn't much there. There was a couple of small plants and a small air base. And, lo and behold, the very next day we're back to the same target. And so three days in a row we went back to Munich. And we were all puzzled. And we finally found out that the reason we went to Munich three days in a row is that Hitler was having one of his famous beer garden meetings down there and they were making him happy or we were making him happy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did you say, was that a nine-hour mission to and from?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: To and from Munich was nine hours.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow. What was your average mission on the B-17?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Well, if you'll look at this list, I'd say the average was in the eights, if you average it out. There were lots of sevens and nines, but about eight or nine hours. On some of those we -- well, on D- -- we flew on D-Day, of course. And that's something I'll never forget because we could see those kids on the beach. I'm saying kids, we were the same age as they. But it seemed like kids to us, you know. It just was awful to see all that bombing and blasting and stuff. And that mission became long because we would fly into France -- over France, you know, and then we'd head out into -- well, that would be west -- out to the ocean and come back up the ocean to England and back to our base. And the reason for that was there was so many aircraft in the air in that period that they had to put us in some kind of a pattern so we wouldn't run into each other. That was -- that was -- D-Day for us was nothing. The Germans didn't put their fighters out. And to this day nobody knows why. So we just flew in and bombed and -- and went around and came back.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What were your targets on D-Day?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Well, it was various emplacements, you know, where they -- where they had their troops gathered. That's where we -- where we were dropping.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Was your bombardier pretty accurate?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: It ended up -- we ended up with two different bombardiers. One got injured and -- and couldn't finish so another guy finished. And they were both good. But, of course, you know, they had that Nordon (ph) bomb site. And basically what we did as a group, we would drop off the lead plane. The lead plane would really pick the spot. And when his -- when he dropped, we dropped. But, nevertheless, our bombardier had to know at all times where he was and what the target was. And if he didn't like it or if it wasn't right, he wouldn't drop. But with us, it was always that way.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You said you had some names for your planes when you did get overseas.

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Yeah. The -- the one that we flew the longest was called "The West Virginian." And it got its name from our crew chief. We had a ground crew, of course, to maintain the airplane. And he said, "We got to name the plane." And we said, "Yeah, that's right. Let's name it." And so we all talked. And none of us could decide what to name it. We didn't know Tom at that time. We wanted to name it "The Wolf," but we didn't know him. But in any case, the chief engineer was from West Virginia. And we said, "Why don't we name it for you?" He said, "You know, I don't want my name on the airplane." "No, we talking about West Virginia." So we named it "The West Virginian." And that's the one that we flew most -- a lot of our missions. That was the name of the .

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How many missions did you do on that one?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: I can't tell you specifically on that one.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember why you had to change? What happened with that plane?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Well, it just -- you know, after a while they just get so many holes in them that you just got to go on to the next one. And once -- that was our first plane, "The West Virginian." And we remember -- I remember the name of that one because it was an unusual thing for -- an unusual experience for me, naming an airplane, you know. But "The West Virginian" was the one. And then after that, I don't remember the names.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you got over there, how many missions did you think you were going to fly?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: When we got there, a tour consisted of 25 missions. Before we got to 25, they changed it to 30. And before we got to 30, they changed it to 35.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the reaction of the crews when they made those changes?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: I don't think it would be kind to put that on tape. Well, you know, it's -- can I tell you what the odds were, and why it was so frustrating? We left Sioux City with 30 crews. That's 10 men to a crew. That's 300 men that went over at the time that we went. And by the time they had changed the tours to where 35 made a tour, of those 300 men, there are only 15 of us. And I thank God I was one of them. There were only 15 of us who actually made 35 missions. So, you know, it can be a little disconcerting.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have memories of buddies that you lost?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: The one that is most memorable was our tail gunner. You know, we flew -- except in the ball they couldn't were a flight vest. But we always flew with flight vests on and a helmet. And our -- the tail gunner, he was -- he was the youngest man in our crew. He was not 19 yet. And his position in the tail, he would kneel back there and look out to the -- to the back. You know, that's where he -- how he worked. Anyhow, one of those unfortunate missions we were really in heavy flak. And at the end of -- whenever we came off a target, everybody had to check in. The tail gun didn't check - did not check in. So the waste guns -- one of the waste gunners said, "I'll go back and look." And he came back and he said, "Burnam is dead." And he and I both -- we were the only two on the crew from Massachusetts, so we had become pretty close friends. He was much younger than I. He was only -- he wasn't 19 yet. So when I got up out of the ball turret, I thought, "I got to go back and see Burnam." I went back to see him, and he was slumped back. He was on his knees, which was his normal position back there, but he was slumped back. And so I -- I moved his head because I couldn't see any -- any marks on him. I moved his head to see, you know, where did he get hit. It was right at the base of his skull a sliver of flak had come up between his vest and his helmet and penetrated his brain. He didn't even bleed. He just bled a little bit. But that's -- that's the fortune of war. But it gives you a very tough feeling.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Is that the only guy that you lost in your crew?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: That's the only one that we lost in death, yeah. We had others. We had -- our engineer, who managed -- who ran the gun on top of the plane, he would stand up in stirrups there to run that and flak got him. It came up through the bottom and came up through his foot into his ankles and so, you know, that took him out. And then we lost one who just broke down. We were getting ready to go on a mission. He was a big guy. It was late in the tour. And he had his hands up on the side of the door to jump in, and he just froze there. He stopped. Anyhow, so I was right behind him. His name was Mike. And he had his hands up there and one foot up on to the plane. So I slapped him, I said, "Come on, Mike. Let's go. We got to get in." And he just -- nothing moved. So I turned around to his side and looked at his face, everything in his face was twitching. He had broken down right there. So that was the end of the ride for him. For the rest of us it was a little nerve racking because they took him away and brought in a substitute waste gunner and we had to go anyway. But the thing that worried us is we took off and headed out into the wild blue, "What did he see? What caused him to break down at that moment? What" -- you know, did he see something that we should know about? You get those strange feelings.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How many missions had he flown before that happened?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: He probably was on -- past midway. He probably was in his 15th or 18th, in that -- in that range.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you thought maybe he had a vision?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: We thought maybe he saw something that the rest of us didn't know about.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow. So did you ever hit anything as a gunner?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Oh, yeah. The clearest one that I got -- the one that I clearly hit, we went on one of those missions where we dropped -- as a whole group, we dropped food, supplies, ammunition and stuff to the free French in Southern France. We were so far down into France that we could see the Alps. That's how far down we were. Anyhow, this thing was obviously prearranged between the free French and the Americans. And they had circles. Each plane carried different things. I forget what we had. I don't remember what, but the circles were colored to indicate armament, food, supplies, you know. And so as we flew down to drop those, we had to hit the right circle. And we went down very low because, you know, they wanted this stuff to last -- to land in good shape. So we dropped at a very low altitude, all of us. And what we -- we went in a big circle, went down, dropped and then would start back up again. As we were starting back up again, a fighter plane -- a German fighter plane appeared, who knows from where. I mean, down in there there was no reason for them to have them. But this guy appeared and -- and he could not have been an -- an experienced fighter pilot because he came at us from the back. Now, you know, the fighter pilot likes to keep speed to his advantage. So they either come to you from above or nose to nose because the speed would close quicker. So coming from the back, he was coming up behind us and -- and he was right in my gun sight and I saw him go down. And you know what, it didn't feel good. And yet it's something that we had to do.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any other confirmed kill that you think you got?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: No. There were many others. Well, we got partials because, you know, they'd be coming at the group and we'd all be shooting. I think my total was like 15.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the toughest of those targets do you think?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Do you mean the bombing?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The bombing of the missions, the toughest missions, other than the one, obviously, over the North Sea. But as far as targets were concerned, fighter cover, flak, that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Any time you get anywhere near Munich, those were tough. They had plenty of fighter coverage. And the flak was thick enough you could walk on it. That's a joke. You couldn't. But it would look like that. You know, there was -- that was -- those were the toughest.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What about the missions to Berlin?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: And Berlin. Yeah, Berlin is -- was well-protected. Heavily protected.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was the feeling when you knew that was the target for the day, though?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Well, first of all, it was a long ride. And, secondly -- let's see, Berlin was eight-and-a-half hours and secondly we knew what we were getting into. Another place where we got heavy coverage and flak and so forth was Stuttgart. They had fighter bases there around, so forth. That was also tough. D-Day, however, was not nasty for us. For some reasons that I don't know and I guess the historians don't know, Hitler did not put his fighters out that day. So we got lots of flak, but we didn't get any -- any real fighter activity.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did he have enough in the area, was that part of the problem?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Maybe that was part of the problem. I have no way of knowing. But all I know is that we were relieved when he didn't have them all up there because those guys were good. I mean, they were not -- but I'll put the Americans ahead of them anytime. Those three fighter pilots that we palled around with on the boat coming back to the States, they told some stories that -- you know. Well, one of the guys who was there, they had -- they had gone out strafing trains. And one of his buddies was telling us the story on this guy. And he was down there strafing so low that his wing actually cut off some telephone poles. He was in a -- in a P-47. First of all, it has to be a pretty tough airplane.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: But can you imagine being down to that -- to that level? But they were great. I think those fighter pilots were just -- not that our pilots were not great, but they were restricted to flying in a group. And the lead plane was the one that took us where we were going. But those fighter pilots, they were gutsy guys.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: From a lot of this you didn't have fighter cover all the way over, right?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: No. They would meet us at certain point -- at a certain point on the mission because they couldn't fly that slow.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Until you got the P-51s, they could go with you, right?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: And the P-51s. The P-51s were our escorts when we got in that trouble over the North Sea. It was the P-51s that happen to be in the area that grouped around us and got us back.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So they escorted you back?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you encounter anybody trying to come after you when you were coming back?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: They had one -- the fighter pilots took off on one occasion. But the thing that really impressed me is that as we were coming back, you could see down to the water, of course, and the air/sea rescue boats were actually down there coming in our direction. Fortunately we didn't need them as it turned out, but they were there. It was pretty well organized.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any other memorable missions that come to mind?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: I think that one of dropping the supplies to the free French is the one that really sticks far out in my mind because we could actually see them down there and we could see them picking up the stuff and...

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: How about getting letters and packages from home, memories of that?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Well, sure. I mean, that was -- we lived for that. I even had letters from my lady in Sioux City, Iowa. And my family kept us in mail and packages. That was a big deal in the barracks, you know. Who got the package today?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Let's get personal. What kinds of things did she write? You couldn't write a whole lot back, right?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Not much.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Other than "I'm fine"?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. So what -- did you know -- they were still cut up, you knew you couldn't write certain things but you just -- did they randomly cut things that you couldn't understand why they cut them?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: I never knew, you know, because it was out of my hands already.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things do you think were missing?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything just hacked off. You figured the mission was over with, why would it matter if you talked about it?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: I know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things did you and your buddies do for entertainment over there?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: We would do crossword puzzles. And if you believe that, I've got another one for you.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Go ahead and tell me.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You drank beer?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: We adopted a dog at our base. And you know what we named it? It's an Italian word, but I'll tell you what it means. We named him -- a little black dog. We named him Umbriago," which is Italian for drunkard. You know, we'd be sitting in the barracks -- and I'd be just drinking pop, you know, but everybody else would be drinking beer. And this dog, he got so -- you know, he wanted to know what we were doing. So we said, "Well, let's give him a little bowl of this." And he used to drink beer with us until he wobbled on his legs. One of saddest things is when we left, we had to leave him there. So we gave him to another crew, but -- but leaving him there was an experience. He was great. So he earned his name, Umbriago.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any U.S. shows come around?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: I never saw one -- one of the big ones. Bob Hope was in our area, but didn't actually come to our base so I didn't get to see him. But, yeah, there were some that came out. Sure.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any memories of your final mission?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Oh, yeah. In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost all the way over. It was -- it was to Hamburg. And other than some flak and stuff, we didn't -- it wasn't very eventful. But it was meaningful to me because I knew that was 35.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you do anything to celebrate when you got back?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: A little. That's when they had the sign on the door. The party went -- the party started as soon as I walked through the door. They have that sign on the door that said, Congrats." They all signed it. And all the liquids that you need for a party were on hand. Well, I've already told you what the odds were, so...

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So in your particular crew did, what, maybe seven of them made it the whole time?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Through the whole tour?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, the whole 35.

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Let me see.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: One guy that got shot in the foot --

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: One broke down.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- the other guy snapped.

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Yeah. I guess about seven of us.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you're a pretty lucky crew?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Yeah. We were better than the average by far -- luckier, I should say, not better. It isn't that we were any better, it's just fate. But, yeah, we did a lot better than most.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you finally come home?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: You mean when did I --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You finished your missions, and when did they send you home?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Well, they didn't send me home. They sent me back to Massachusetts to become a trainer, to teach me how to do that. And from Massachusetts they sent me to Las Vegas, Nevada, to be training the crews down there. I got to tell you this final thing about -- and then that's when Lavern came out and we were married. But other than that very significant event, the one that I remember most clearly, the rumors had started that -- you know, there were a number of us who had completed tours who were doing the training back there on that Las Vegas air base. And the word came out that the command was thinking that what they should do is take some of the experienced gunners from the European Theater and put them on these B-29s so we could get better activity. And that did not make any of us very happy. First of all, the few of us that were around had beaten terrible odds. And now to try and go do another one just didn't seem like it -- like it fit well.

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: They were going to put us on a B-29. And then Harry Truman, against the advice of all the smart people, dropped that bomb -- the atom bomb on Nagasaki, I guess it was.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Hiroshima?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Hiroshima. And, of course, that changed the whole war. And I can't tell you this on tape.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you want to stop?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So about -- about when would you have come back to Massachusetts? Would that be late '44 or early '45?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: We were married in --

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It was '45?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: We were married in '45, were we? No, '44.

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: '45, yeah, because I was in Europe in '44.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When's your anniversary?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: April the 1st.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay. So you probably got back in the spring of '45 sometime, and you were married in Vegas, right?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: No, I was still in the service. St. Joan of Arc, if you want to know the name of the church.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It's still there?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: It's still there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you think about that experience overseas, does any particularly -- any other particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Nothing at this very moment that's different or unusual.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else we haven't covered?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: No, I think we pretty well covered it, as far as I remember.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, you've done great.

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: You're a good audience.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you have any trouble adjusting when you got back?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: I think you'd have to ask my wife. I don't remember any.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Didn't want to be?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: I did have some claustrophobia, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you eventually get over that?

sp.speaker: Phillip C. Vincello
sp.p: Pretty much.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Well, I can imagine why that was the case.
